Empirical Research Plan: “Is the supply of bank credit cyclical – independent of loan demand?”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Method: Difference-in-Differences with firm-*bank* fixed effects (a “within-borrower, across-lender, across-time” DID).  
Core idea: in recessions, banks whose balance sheets are ex-ante weak (low Tier-1 capital, high wholesale funding share) should contract lending more than otherwise similar banks whose balance sheets are strong. Because we compare the *same firm* borrowing from differentially-exposed banks over time, we difference out changes in the firm’s loan demand and isolate credit-supply movements.

The design is analogous to Khwaja-Mian (QJE 2008): use multiple-bank relationships to hold borrower demand constant but add a business-cycle interaction to ask whether the contraction is *cyclical*. Formally,

LoanOutcome_{fbtq} = β1 (WeakBank_b × Recession_q) + γ_fbt + λ_fq + θ_b + ε_{fbtq}

where β1 captures the incremental recession-period contraction among weak banks relative to strong banks for the *same* firm in the same quarter.

Suitability:
• DID is ideal because we have panel data for the same borrower across many banks and many quarters.  
• The interaction (WeakBank × Recession) yields the “treatment” that turns on only when the macro shock occurs, giving us a clean before/after comparison.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable
  WeakBank_b = 1 if bank b’s Tier-1 capital ratio in t–1q is below the 25th percentile of all lead‐arranger banks (or if wholesale-funding share > 75th pct). Results will be reported for both definitions.

Control group
  StrongBank_b = 0 if bank b’s Tier-1 ratio is above median (or wholesale funding < median).  

Treatment timing
  Recession_q = 1 if quarter q is classified as an NBER recession; 0 otherwise. Thus the DID “switches on” only when WeakBank = 1 *and* Recession = 1.

Sample construction
  Keep only firms that borrow from ≥2 lead banks over the sample window so the same firm can appear with both treated and control lenders.

Outcome variables
  a. ln(LoanAmount)  
  b. All-in-drawn spread (bps)  
  c. Indicator that the firm issues a bond in the same quarter (reveals substitution).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends: Absent a recession, lending by weak vs. strong banks to the same borrower would have followed parallel paths. Plausibility: with firm×time fixed effects, we difference *within* firm×quarter, so only within-quarter relative outcomes remain; pre-trend tests using only expansion periods can be reported.

A2. No borrower-specific shocks differentially correlated with weak banks exactly in recessions. Since the same borrower is observed with both weak and strong banks in the *same quarter*, contemporaneous borrower shocks are differenced out.

A3. Bank weakness predates the recession (predetermined). We measure WeakBank using lagged (t–1q) balance sheet data, well before loan negotiation, limiting reverse causality.

A4. Stable composition of multiple-bank borrowers: the set of firms with multiple relationships is not itself a cyclical outcome of bank weakness. We will test robustness by (i) conditioning on firms that had multiple relationships pre-sample, and (ii) inverse-probability weights for the propensity to have multiple banks.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigations
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Threat 1. Selection of borrowers to weak banks changes in recessions (e.g., weaker firms purposely seek weaker banks).  
• Mitigation: borrower×quarter fixed effects mean that *within the same quarter* we compare simultaneous loans to the same borrower; selection cannot vary within the quarter.  

Threat 2. Measurement error in Tier-1 ratio mis-classifies treatment, biasing β1 toward zero.  
• Mitigation: use multiple balance-sheet proxies (capital ratio, wholesale funding share, securitisation reliance); instrument WeakBank with its pre-1998 average to create a leave-one-out predicted value.

Threat 3. Loan supply changes are contaminated by aggregate capital-market shocks (bond market also shuts).  
• Mitigation: include quarter fixed effects (λ_q) and control for option-adjusted corporate bond spreads; additionally run the outcome “loan-spread minus bond-spread (same firm-quarter)” which nets out broad capital-market conditions.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# Load packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)    # fast high-dim FE regressions
library(lmtest); library(sandwich)

# 1. Load data -------------------------------------------------------
loans <- fread("dealscan_matched.csv")      # loan-level panel
banks <- fread("call_reports.csv")          # quarterly bank data
nber  <- fread("nber_recessions_quarterly.csv")
bonds <- fread("sdc_bond_issues.csv")

# 2. Merge & construct variables ------------------------------------
# Bank weakness (lagged)
banks[, WeakBank := fifelse(Tier1_Capital < quantile(Tier1_Capital, .25, na.rm=TRUE), 1, 0), 
      by = quarter]
banks[, bank_q := paste0(bank_id,"_",quarter)]
loans[, bank_q := paste0(lead_bank_id,"_",quarter)]

panel <- merge(loans, banks[, .(bank_q, WeakBank, Tier1_Capital)], by="bank_q", all.x=TRUE)

# Recession indicator
panel <- merge(panel, nber, by="quarter", all.x=TRUE)  # Recession_q variable

# Keep firms with ≥2 banks ever
multi_rel <- panel[, uniqueN(lead_bank_id), by=borrower_id][V1>=2, borrower_id]
panel <- panel[borrower_id %in% multi_rel]

# Outcomes
panel[, lnLoanAmt := log(loan_amount)]
panel[, spread_bps := all_in_drawn_spread]

# 3. DID main regression --------------------------------------------
feols_main <- feols(lnLoanAmt ~ WeakBank*Recession_q | 
                    borrower_id + quarter + lead_bank_id, data=panel, 
                    cluster = ~borrower_id)
summary(feols_main)

# Alternative outcome: spread
feols_spread <- feols(spread_bps ~ WeakBank*Recession_q | 
                      borrower_id + quarter + lead_bank_id, data=panel, 
                      cluster = ~borrower_id)

# 4. Robustness: leave-one-out predicted WeakBank -------------------
pre98 <- banks[year < 1998, .(preWeak = mean(WeakBank, na.rm=TRUE)), by=bank_id]
panel <- merge(panel, pre98, by="bank_id", all.x=TRUE)

feols_iv <- feols(lnLoanAmt ~ Recession_q | borrower_id + quarter + lead_bank_id |
                  (WeakBank ~ preWeak*Recession_q), data=panel, cluster=~borrower_id)
summary(feols_iv)

# 5. Event-study pre-trend check ------------------------------------
panel[, rel_q := quarter_distance_to_recession]  # e.g., –8,…,8
event <- feols(lnLoanAmt ~ i(rel_q, WeakBank, ref=-1) | borrower_id + lead_bank_id + quarter,
               data=panel[abs(rel_q)<=8], cluster=~borrower_id)
iplot(event)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Theory predicts β1 < 0 for loan amounts and β1 > 0 for loan spreads: weak-capital banks cut loan supply in recessions, charging higher prices or simply shrinking quantity relative to strong banks. Magnitude (ballpark): a 25 % lower Tier-1 ratio leads to 10–15 % lower loan volumes during recessions and 30–50 bp higher spreads, consistent with prior estimates on bank capital shocks.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment
(1 = clearly satisfied; 0 = questionable)
C1: Predetermined treatment (WeakBank measured pre-shock) .............. 1  
C2: Parallel trends (supported by event-study pre-period) .............. 0.8  
C3: No simultaneous policy differences across banks .................... 0.8  
C4: No spillovers across firms or banks (SUTVA) ........................ 0.7  
C5: Robustness to alternative treatment definitions ................... 1  

Average ≈ 0.86 → overall design appears credible but still sensitive to borrower–bank matching dynamics and potential spillovers in syndicated loans.
